result: The manuscript provides background on IBD genetics, noting that IBD affects 1.5-3 million people in the US, is genetically determined with over 200 GWAS-identified risk variants (mostly intergenic with modest effect), and over 50 genes linked to early-onset IBD, yet 20-30% of genetic risk remains unexplained.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C11-C16 provide well-established background information about IBD epidemiology and genetics, supported by appropriate citations and general knowledge. These contextual claims are accurate and properly referenced.

result: The manuscript describes the intestinal environment and specialized cell populations, including that the intestine has the largest epithelial surface and microbiota concentration, contains the most immune cells, and houses enteroendocrine cells (EECs, 1% of epithelium) and gut neurons that form neuro-epithelial circuits.
evaluation: Claims C17-C28 provide established background on intestinal anatomy, cell populations, and their functions, all supported by appropriate citations. This contextual information is well-documented in the literature.

result: A consanguineous Hispanic family was identified with three of five children affected by early-onset ulcerative colitis, diagnosed at ages 6-8 by standard criteria, with two siblings showing severe pancolonic disease requiring colectomy and one showing milder rectal disease controlled by mesalamine.
evaluation: Claims C29-C34 describe the clinical presentation of the index family, supported by clinical data, pedigree information (Figure 1a), endoscopic images (Figure 1b), and clinical timeline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The clinical characterization is well-documented.

result: Genetic analysis identified a homozygous SCGN p.R77H variant (rs376721140; NM_006998.3:c.230G>A) segregating with disease in the family, located in shared LOH regions on chromosome 6, confirmed as the only rare homozygous nonsynonymous variant in LOH segments by WES and WGS, with proper familial segregation validated by Sanger sequencing.
evaluation: Claims C35-C40 describe the genetic discovery process using SNP arrays, WES, WGS, and Sanger sequencing. The data are presented in Table 1, Figure 1a, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The multi-platform approach and segregation analysis provide strong evidence for the variant identification.

result: The SCGN p.R77H variant is ultra-rare with allele frequencies of 0.014% (ExAC overall), 0.017% (ExAC Hispanics), and 0.025% (Dallas Heart Study Hispanics), with no homozygous individuals identified in any database.
evaluation: Claims C41-C43 document the rarity of the variant using multiple population databases. The frequencies are consistent with a rare recessive disease allele, and the absence of homozygotes in large databases supports pathogenicity.

result: The SCGN p.R77H variant affects a highly conserved arginine at position 77 in the predicted second EF-hand domain of secretagogin (a calcium-sensing protein with 6 EF-hand domains), and this residue shows limited coding variation in ExAC, suggesting functional importance.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1c), allele frequency analysis (Figure 1d), and citation to Wagner et al., 2000. The conservation analysis and low allelic variation support potential functional significance of the affected residue.

result: SCGN is expressed in scattered triangularly-shaped epithelial cells (morphologically compatible with EECs) in human rectal biopsies, with expression pattern unchanged in patient tissues. In mouse intestine, SCGN partially co-localizes with EEC markers (CGA, CGB, 5-HT, GCG) marking a unique EEC subpopulation, and is also expressed in gut neurons co-staining with neuronal markers (TUJ1, SNAP25, SYP). In pancreatic islets, SCGN shows uniform expression with complete CGA co-localization.
evaluation: Claims C47-C53 describe SCGN expression patterns supported by immunohistochemistry (Figure 2a-b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 2c-f, Figure 2—figure supplements 2-3). The morphometric quantification (Figure 2d) and citation to Haber et al., 2017 support the characterization of SCGN-expressing cell populations.

result: SCGN interacts with SNARE complex components SNAP23 and SNAP25. CRISPR/Cas9-generated Scgn knockout STC-1 cell clones showed significantly reduced DHA-stimulated GLP-1 secretion compared to parental cells, and cells expressing SCGNR77H showed significantly impaired GLP-1 secretion compared to wild-type SCGN rescue, indicating the variant is a hypomorphic allele affecting secretion dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by citations (Bauer et al., 2011; Rogstam et al., 2007), western blot validation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and GLP-1 secretion assays (Figure 3a-b). The functional data demonstrate both loss of SCGN and the R77H variant impair hormone secretion, though statistical significance is shown.

result: SCGNR77H retains binding to SNAP25 by co-immunoprecipitation but fails to properly localize SNAP25 to the plasma membrane. In parental cells, both SCGN and SNAP25 show vesicular and plasma membrane localization, but SNAP25 membrane localization is lost in Scgn KO cells and restored by wild-type SCGN but not by SCGNR77H. The R77H variant itself also fails to localize to the plasma membrane, indicating abnormal subcellular localization affecting SNAP25 and ultimately SNARE function.
evaluation: Claims C59-C65 are supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and immunofluorescence imaging with quantification (Figure 3c-d). The data demonstrate that while protein-protein interaction is maintained, subcellular localization is disrupted, providing a mechanistic explanation for functional impairment.

result: In zebrafish (73% identical ortholog), SCGN suppression by morpholino caused reduced midbrain size, which was rescued by human SCGNWT mRNA but not by SCGNR77H mRNA, demonstrating that SCGNR77H is devoid of normal activity in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showing the developmental phenotype and differential rescue by wild-type versus mutant SCGN. This provides in vivo validation that R77H is a loss-of-function allele.

result: Two independent Scgn knockout mouse lines (Secret1 and Secret2) were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 targeting exon 3, resulting in truncated transcripts and loss of SCGN protein expression. At baseline, Scgn-deficient mice showed no overt phenotype, normal colonic architecture, intact epithelial cell markers, and no differences in microbiota diversity or composition compared to wild-type mice.
evaluation: Claims C71-C76 are supported by genotyping data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-b), RT-PCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c-d), immunofluorescence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e), histology (Figure 4a), qRT-PCR (Figure 4b), and 16S rRNA sequencing (Figure 4c-e). The baseline characterization is thorough and well-documented.

result: Upon DSS administration, Scgn-deficient mice (Secret1 and Secret2 lines) showed increased susceptibility to colitis with worse weight loss, elevated disease activity index, greater mortality, increased histological damage, and elevated pro-inflammatory gene expression compared to wild-type mice. This phenotype was observed in male-only and mixed-gender cohorts and in both independent knockout lines. Baseline lamina propria leukocyte populations showed no differences between genotypes.
evaluation: Claims C77-C86 are supported by weight loss data (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b), disease activity index (Figure 5b), survival curves (Figure 5c), histological scoring (Figure 5d-e), and qRT-PCR of inflammatory markers (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c). Flow cytometry data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) show no baseline immune differences. The colitis phenotype is replicated across two independent lines and multiple experimental conditions.

result: Colonic EEC ablation was achieved using CDX2-Cre to delete Neurog3 in colonocytes, resulting in loss of CGA-positive cells and EEC-specific gene expression (including Scgn) in the colon but not small intestine, confirmed by immunofluorescence, qRT-PCR, and RNA-seq. Functionally, Neurog3ΔCol mice showed drastically reduced baseline and DHA-stimulated GLP-1 and GLP-2 secretion from colon explants, similar to the blunted response in Secret1 mice.
evaluation: Claims C87-C94 are supported by breeding strategy diagram (Figure 6a), immunofluorescence (Figure 6b), qRT-PCR (Figure 6c), RNA-seq heatmap (Figure 6d), and ex-vivo hormone secretion assays (Figure 6e). The EEC ablation model is well-characterized and functionally validated.

result: EEC-deficient (Neurog3ΔCol) mice did not show increased susceptibility to DSS-induced colitis, suggesting that colonic EECs do not mediate the immunomodulatory effects of SCGN and raising the possibility that SCGN-expressing enteric neurons may modulate intestinal immune homeostasis.
evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by DSS colitis data (Figure 6f-g) showing no difference between Neurog3f/f and Neurog3ΔCol mice. This is a critical negative result that redirects the mechanistic interpretation from EECs to neurons. However, C97 is speculative and requires future validation with neuron-specific models.

result: The patients with SCGN mutations displayed only colitis without other clinically overt phenotypes (unlike other monogenic IBD forms), normal fasting glycemia (unlike Scgn-deficient mice that develop diabetes), and no neurocognitive phenotypes (unlike zebrafish/mouse models). SCGN protein is absent from the immune system, pointing to neuroendocrine cells as the source of pathology.
evaluation: Claims C98-C102 are based on clinical observations and comparisons to other disease models and SCGN expression patterns. The citations to Malenczyk et al., 2017; Deciphering Developmental Disorders Study, 2015; Hanics et al., 2017; and Meeths et al., 2010 support the comparisons. The phenotypic differences between humans and animal models are notable but may reflect species differences or incomplete penetrance.

result: The manuscript discusses potential roles for EECs and gut neurons in immune regulation, noting that EECs express Toll-like receptors and receptors for microbial metabolites that can stimulate hormone secretion, and that murine models of gut neuron/glial defects and human gut neuron deficiency (Hirschsprung's disease) are associated with colitis.
evaluation: Claims C103-C105 provide literature context supported by appropriate citations (Bogunovic et al., 2007; Lebrun et al., 2017; Palazzo et al., 2007; Selleri et al., 2008; Bush et al., 1998; Cheng et al., 2010; Fujimoto et al., 1988; Demehri et al., 2013; Gosain, 2016; Gosain and Brinkman, 2015). This background supports the biological plausibility of the findings.

result: The manuscript concludes that the ultra-rare SCGN p.R77H variant causes Mendelian early-onset ulcerative colitis, that functional deficiency in SCGN can result in intestinal inflammation, and that this implicates the neuroendocrine cellular compartment in IBD.
evaluation: Claims C4, C9, and C10 represent the main conclusions. While the genetic, cellular, and mouse data are strong, establishing causality for a Mendelian disease typically requires: (1) multiple unrelated families with the same phenotype and gene, (2) functional rescue experiments in patient cells, or (3) engineered models recapitulating the exact variant. The study presents one family, and while the mouse knockout and cellular models support loss of function, the specific R77H variant's effects are only tested in cell culture and zebrafish. The conclusion that this variant "causes" disease is strongly supported but not definitively proven by current standards. Additional families or patient-derived cell rescue experiments would strengthen causality claims.
